# SK0231 — The string call produces the string it was given

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`ToString()` on a string, `foreach` over `ToCharArray()`, `string.Format` of a literal with no placeholders, an interpolated string with no holes, and a verbatim prefix that escapes nothing.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Cleanup |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

Two of the five are allocations rather than noise. `s.ToCharArray()` copies the whole string so that `foreach` can walk what `string` already enumerates by index, and `string.Format` runs a format parser over a format that has no items. The other three are the reader's cost: a `$` promises a hole, a `@` promises something that needs escaping, and a `.ToString()` on a string promises a conversion. Each one is a sentence that turns out to say nothing, and a reader has to finish it before finding that out.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
foreach (var c in line.ToCharArray()) {
    Consume(c);
}

var label = string.Format("unnamed") + name.ToString();
```

Write:

```csharp
foreach (var c in line) {
    Consume(c);
}

var label = "unnamed" + name;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Each branch is guarded by what the deletion would mean, not by what it would look like.** An interpolated string is reported only where the compiler was converting it to `string`: `FormattableString fs = $"a";` and every interpolated-string-handler overload accept `$"a"` and reject `"a"`, and nothing in the syntax separates the two. `string.Format` is reported only where the literal holds no brace at all, because `string.Format("{{0}}")` returns `{0}` and the literal returns `{{0}}` — the shape that looks most obviously safe is the one that is not. A verbatim prefix is reported only where the body holds no backslash, no doubled quote and no newline, since the prefix is what makes each of those mean what it means. ⚠ `s.ToString();` as a whole statement is the null-check idiom and is never reported: the result is discarded, so the dereference *is* the call, and `s;` is not an expression statement. ⚠ A receiver the compiler's flow analysis says may be null is left alone in both call shapes, because `s.ToString()` is typed `string` where `s` is `string?` and the deletion is where `CS8600` would come from. ⚠ **Three of the family's eight inspections are deliberately not covered.** `RedundantToStringCallForValueType` is not: `$"{d}"` on an `IFormattable` calls `ToString(null, provider)` where `d.ToString()` calls `ToString()`, and a supplied provider makes those two different strings. `RedundantStringInterpolation`'s single-hole form is not: `$"{x}"` is `""` where `x` is null and `x` is null, which is a change of value and not of spelling. `RedundantStringType` and `RedundantVerbatimPrefix`'s identifier form are not covered either — the identifier form neighbours `SK2034`. ⚠ The receiver's type is read from the symbol and never from the written name, so `((object)s).ToString()` and `count.ToString()` are both left alone.
